chapters.title: Chapter 6: Using Financial Statements at Work

lessons.title: Case Study: Reading a Real Indian Company's Annual Report as a Manager

children.text: Everything in this course now gets used at once. You are still the manager at Kesari Foods, the ₹50 crore Indore snacks company. Your managing director wants to know how the business compares with the listed leader in the category, and she wants it in ninety minutes, not a consulting project.

The company you will read is Britannia Industries, listed on NSE and BSE, for the year ended 31 March 2025. Every figure below comes from its consolidated numbers as published on screener.in. Work through it in order, because the sequence is the method.

body.text: Reading an annual report well is not about understanding everything. It is about asking six questions in the right order and stopping when they are answered.

events.title: Get the documents
events.description: Open the company page on screener.in for ten years of data, and download the annual report from the investor relations page or the exchange for the notes.

events.title: Read the P&L
events.description: Revenue, growth, the margin ladder, and every expense line as a percentage of revenue for two years.

events.title: Read the balance sheet
events.description: Net worth, borrowings, and how much capital is tied up in working capital and fixed assets.

events.title: Read the cash flow statement
events.description: The sign pattern, operating cash against profit, and what the cash was spent on.

events.title: Compute the ratios
events.description: Margins, ROCE, working capital days, debt to equity, interest coverage, for both companies.

events.title: Write the five findings
events.description: What is different, why, and which differences your own company can act on.

children.text: Step 1: The Profit and Loss Read

stats.label: Operating profit
stats.context: 17.7% of revenue, before depreciation and interest

children.text: The first observation is one you now make automatically: revenue grew 7.0% and profit grew 2.1%. Something between the two lines grew faster than sales, which is the question to carry into the notes and the management discussion.
Step 2: The Balance Sheet Read

stats.label: Net worth
stats.context: Equity capital ₹24 crore plus reserves ₹4,332 crore

stats.label: Asset turnover
stats.context: Every rupee of assets produces ₹2.03 of sales

children.text: Note the relationship that Kesari Foods does not have. Britannia generates twice its asset base in annual revenue. Kesari generates ₹50 crore of revenue on ₹48 crore of assets, which is 1.04 times. Same industry, and one company works its capital twice as hard.
Step 3: The Cash Flow Read

body.caption: Britannia FY25 cash flow by activity (₹ crore)

cells: More cash than the ₹2,178 crore of profit, so earnings are being collected
Net inflow, as maturing investments exceeded capital spending
Cash returned to shareholders and lenders
Cash fell slightly, by choice rather than by pressure

body.text: This is the mature self-funding pattern from Lesson 4.2. Operations produced ₹2,491 crore, the business needed almost none of it for new capacity, and ₹2,754 crore went back out to shareholders and lenders. A company in this position does not need to ask anyone for permission to have a bad year.

body.title: Run the quality of earnings test
body.prompt: Britannia reported cash from operating activities of ₹2,491 crore and profit after tax of ₹2,178 crore in FY25. What is the ratio of operating cash to profit?
body.explanation: ₹2,491 crore ÷ ₹2,178 crore = 1.14. Above 1 means the company collects more cash than it reports as profit, which is what you want to see. Kesari Foods managed 0.73, because ₹6 crore of its profit went into receivables.

children.text: Step 4: The Ratios, Side by Side

body.caption: Kesari Foods against Britannia Industries, FY25

cells: Not comparable in scale, which is fine
Remarkably close. Kesari is not badly run on cost
The gap opens below EBITDA: interest and depreciation
Three times better, and this is the finding that matters
Half the sales per rupee of assets
Less than half the stock, for the same kind of product
Kesari stretches suppliers far harder, and still has worse cash
Britannia is paid before it pays
One collects its profits, the other funds its customers

body.title: Working capital cycle: days of cash tied up

body.text: Resist the obvious conclusion that Kesari should copy the 9-day receivable cycle. Britannia sells through a distribution system built over decades, with brands strong enough that distributors pay upfront to hold stock. The lesson is not the number. It is that bargaining power shows up as working capital, and working capital shows up as ROCE.

children.text: Step 5: The Finding Behind the Finding
The two companies earn nearly the same EBITDA margin. One earns 17.6% on its capital and the other 53%. If margin is not the explanation, the explanation must sit in the denominator, and it does.
Working capital:

Kesari ties up 60 days of cash in its cycle while Britannia releases cash, because it collects in 9 days and pays in 60. At ₹50 crore of revenue, closing even half the receivable gap would release several crore.
Asset intensity:
Britannia produces ₹2.03 of sales per rupee of assets against Kesari's ₹1.04, partly through outsourced manufacturing that keeps plants off its own balance sheet.
Leverage and its cost:

Kesari's debt to equity of 0.62 against Britannia's 0.29 means interest consumes a much larger share of its operating profit, which is why the two net margins diverge even though the EBITDA margins do not.

body.title: Where the difference sat
body.textWithBlank: Two companies with nearly identical EBITDA margins can report very different returns on capital, because ROCE also depends on the ___ employed in the business.
body.explanation: ROCE is operating profit over capital employed. When margins match, the entire difference comes from how much capital each company needs to produce that profit, which is mostly working capital and fixed assets.

body.title: What do you take to your MD?
body.question: You have ninety minutes of work and one slide. Which finding should lead?
options: Britannia is 350 times larger, so comparison is not meaningful
Our EBITDA margin is close to Britannia's, but our ROCE is a third of theirs, and the gap is working capital and asset intensity rather than cost control
Britannia's earnings per share is ₹90.45 against our unlisted position
Britannia grew revenue 7.0% while our growth was different
body.explanation: It is specific, it is actionable, and it tells leadership where not to look. Cost cutting will not close this gap, because the cost structures are already similar. Collections, inventory and asset utilisation will.

children.text: Step 6: The Five Questions to Take Back
What would our ROCE be if receivable days fell from 88 to 60, and who owns that change?
How much of our ₹7 crore of inventory has not moved in six months, and what is the cost of clearing it?
Are we stretching suppliers to 126 days because we negotiated it, or because we have no cash, and does that breach the 45-day rule for micro and small suppliers?
Which of our assets earn nothing, and could they be sold, sublet or better utilised?
If our EBITDA margin is already near the category leader's, what exactly is our plan to close the returns gap, expressed in days and rupees rather than in adjectives?

body.title: Ninety minutes, one page, your own employer
body.scenario: Repeat the exercise on your own company or one you are considering joining, supplying or acquiring. You have the statements, the six-step sequence, and one page to present.
body.prompt: What does your one page contain, and what does it deliberately leave out?
body.modelAnswer:
What the page contains:
1. A one-line description of what the business does and how it earns money, so that the numbers have context.
2. Three years of revenue, EBITDA margin, net margin and ROCE, as a small table, not a paragraph.
3. The working capital cycle in days, with each of the three components shown separately so the cause is visible.
4. Operating cash against profit for the same three years, as the quality of earnings check.
5. Debt to equity and interest coverage, with a note on any borrowing due within twelve months.
6. The two or three findings, each written as a cause and a consequence, with the rupee value attached.
7. One recommendation with an owner and a date.
What it deliberately leaves out:
8. Every ratio that does not change a decision. Nobody needs eleven ratios on a page that supports one recommendation.
9. The company's own adjectives from the annual report, such as robust, resilient and strategic. They carry no information.
10. Precision that the data does not support. Rounded figures with a stated basis beat two decimal places built on a guess.
11. Anything you have not verified in the statements, because the first number that cannot be traced to a source is the one you will be asked about.

body.title: Your turn, on a real company
steps: Pick a listed company in your own industry and open its consolidated statements for the last three years.
Compute the margin ladder, ROCE, asset turnover and working capital days for each year.
Compute operating cash to profit for each year and note the trend.
Read the auditor's opinion, the related party note and the contingent liabilities note.
Compare each ratio against your own employer and mark the three largest gaps.
Write the one finding you would put in front of your MD, with a number and an owner attached.

body.title: How you read a company now

columns.label: Before this course
points: Revenue and profit are the only numbers that register
The annual report is 300 pages of noise
Cash and profit are assumed to be the same thing
A cost overrun is judged against the original budget
A business case is an argument

columns.label: After it
points: Margin ladder, ROCE and working capital days in ten minutes
The notes are the destination, not an appendix
Profit is an opinion, cash is a fact, and you can bridge the two
Variances are flexed and split by cause before anyone is blamed
A business case is cash flows, a hurdle rate and a stated downside

cards.definition: P&L for the period, balance sheet on a date, cash flow statement explaining the movement between them.
Profit less dividends flows to equity, closing cash equals balance sheet cash, and balance sheet movements build the cash flow statement.
Gross, EBITDA, operating, pre-tax and net. Match the rung to the decision.
Inventory days plus receivable days minus payable days. The days your cash is out of the business.
Operating profit over capital employed, compared against the cost of that capital.
Operating cash divided by profit after tax, read over three years.
The budget restated at actual volume, before any cost variance is judged.
Incremental cash flows, a hurdle rate, a payback, and the break-even level of benefit.

points: Read any company in six steps: documents, P&L, balance sheet, cash flow, ratios, findings.
Britannia and Kesari earn similar EBITDA margins, and Britannia earns three times the return on capital.
When margins match, the entire difference in returns sits in capital employed: working capital and asset intensity.
A negative cash conversion cycle means a company is paid before it pays, which is bargaining power expressed as cash.
Operating cash above profit, low debt and cash returned to shareholders is the signature of a self-funding business.
Finish every analysis with findings that carry a number, an owner and a date, and leave out every ratio that changes nothing.

body.text: Kesari Foods is fictional and its figures were constructed across this course for teaching. Britannia Industries figures are FY25 consolidated numbers as published on screener.in, and ratios such as ROCE differ slightly depending on whether year-end or average capital is used. This is an educational comparison, not investment advice or a recommendation on any security.
